question: In the test pyramid, unit tests are at the base. What does this mean for the CI pipeline?

options.text: Unit tests should run last — they are the most important
options.explanation: The opposite. Test importance does not determine order. Unit tests run first precisely because they are fast — the fail-fast principle.

options.text: Unit tests should run first — they are fast and provide early feedback
options.explanation: Correct. Unit tests run in seconds, require no external dependencies. Failure at unit tests immediately signals a problem, without wasting time on slow E2E.

options.text: Pipeline position is not related to the test pyramid — these are different concepts
options.explanation: The test pyramid directly influences pipeline structure. The fail-fast principle dictates: fast cheap tests first, slow expensive tests later.

options.text: Unit tests run in parallel with E2E to save time
options.explanation: This is technically possible, but defeats the fail-fast principle. If unit tests fail, there is no point wasting resources on E2E.

question: You added the postgres:15-alpine service in GitLab CI. How to connect to it from a test job?

options.text: At localhost:5432 — all services are available on localhost
options.explanation: localhost works in GitHub Actions (with port forwarding), but not in GitLab CI. In GitLab, services are available by image name.

options.text: At postgres:5432 — hostname = image name without tag
options.explanation: Correct. GitLab CI creates a separate Docker network. The service postgres:15-alpine is available as host 'postgres'. If you need a different name — use alias.

options.text: At service.postgres:5432 — GitLab adds a 'service' prefix
options.explanation: There is no prefix. Host = image name without tag and without path (postgresql becomes postgres, my-registry.com/postgres:15 becomes postgres).

options.text: At 127.0.0.1:5432 — loopback is always available
options.explanation: Loopback refers to the job container itself, not the service container. PostgreSQL runs in a separate container.

question: What does artifacts:reports:junit do in GitLab CI and why is artifacts:when: always needed?

options.text: always is needed so artifacts are not deleted after expire_in
options.explanation: when and expire_in are different settings. when determines under what job outcome to save the artifact. expire_in determines how long to keep it.

options.text: junit tells GitLab to parse XML and show tests in the MR; always is needed to see details of failed tests
options.explanation: Exactly. artifacts:reports:junit parses JUnit XML and displays results in the Tests tab in the MR. when: always is critical — without it the file won't be saved on job failure (default is on_success), and the MR won't show which tests failed.

options.text: junit specifies a path for saving the test execution log
options.explanation: artifacts:paths is used for arbitrary files. artifacts:reports:junit is a special type that signals GitLab about the format and processing method.

options.text: junit sends a Slack notification with test results
options.explanation: JUnit has nothing to do with notifications. It's an XML file format with test results that GitLab can parse and display in the UI.

question: You use parallel: 4 to speed up tests. The job starts and completes successfully, but all 4 shards run the same tests. What is the error?

options.text: You need to manually create 4 separate jobs with different names
options.explanation: You could, but that doesn't solve the problem of running the same tests. The key is to pass sharding parameters to the test framework, and parallel: 4 is perfectly suited for that.

options.text: parallel value cannot be more than 2 in free GitLab
options.explanation: There is no restriction on the parallel value by plan type. Limitations concern CI minutes and runners, but not the parallel keyword itself.

options.text: parallel: 4 only works with Python, Node.js needs a different approach
options.explanation: parallel: 4 is a GitLab mechanism independent of language. The problem is that the job script does not use CI_NODE_INDEX and CI_NODE_TOTAL variables.

options.text: The script does not use CI_NODE_INDEX/CI_NODE_TOTAL to split tests into shards
options.explanation: Correct. parallel: 4 only launches 4 copies of the job and passes variables CI_NODE_INDEX (1,2,3,4) and CI_NODE_TOTAL (4). The test framework itself must use them: jest --shard=$CI_NODE_INDEX/$CI_NODE_TOTAL or pytest --splits=$CI_NODE_TOTAL --group=$CI_NODE_INDEX.

question: A test suite takes 20 minutes. With parallel: 5, what is the expected execution time (with uniform test distribution)?

options.text: 100 minutes — 5 copies of 20 minutes each
options.explanation: That would be the case if parallel: 5 ran all tests in each shard. But the point is to split tests into shards — then each executes only a portion.

options.text: 20 minutes — parallel does not affect total time, only load
options.explanation: parallel is exactly for reducing time. With 5 parallel shards, each executes 1/5 of the tests.

options.text: 4 minutes — each of 5 shards executes 1/5 of tests in parallel
options.explanation: Correct. 20 minutes / 5 shards = 4 minutes (assuming 5 available runners and uniformly distributed tests). This is 5x faster.

options.text: 1 minute — GitLab automatically optimizes test distribution
options.explanation: GitLab does not know about individual test execution times. It only passes CI_NODE_INDEX, and the test framework splits tests evenly by count, not by time.

question: The team notices that a test fails in CI with 'connection refused' to PostgreSQL, but everything works locally. Which TWO actions will fix the situation?

options.text: Add POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD: trust to the job variables
options.explanation: POSTGRES_HOST_AUTH_METHOD: trust simplifies authentication (no password needed), but does not solve 'connection refused'. This error means the port is unreachable, not an authentication rejection.

options.text: Add service readiness wait: until pg_isready -h postgres; do sleep 1; done
options.explanation: Correct. PostgreSQL takes several seconds to start. Tests run before the service accepts connections. Waiting for readiness solves the race condition.

options.text: Change DATABASE_URL from localhost to postgres (service name)
options.explanation: Correct. This is a classic mistake. Locally you use localhost, in GitLab CI you use the service container name (postgres, redis, etc.).

options.text: Switch from Docker executor to Shell executor — services are not supported in Docker
options.explanation: Wrong. services work specifically with Docker executor. Shell executor does not support services at all.

question: Which coverage: regex correctly parses Jest output like 'Lines : 85.32% ( 1247/1463 )'?

options.text: coverage: 'Lines'
options.explanation: A simple string won't work as a regex for extracting a number. GitLab needs a capture group (parentheses) to get the numeric value.

options.text: coverage: '/85/'
options.explanation: A hardcoded number won't work across different runs. The regex must dynamically extract the percentage from the output.

options.text: coverage: '/Lines\s*:\s*(\d+\.?\d*)%/'
options.explanation: Correct. \s* allows spaces around the colon, (\d+\.?\d*) is a capture group with a number (integer or decimal). GitLab takes exactly the first capture group as the coverage value.

options.text: coverage: '/coverage: (\d+)/'
options.explanation: This pattern won't match Jest output. Jest outputs 'Lines : 85.32%', not 'coverage: 85'.

question: You set up parallel:matrix to test three Node.js versions (18, 20, 22) and two databases (sqlite, postgres). How many jobs will GitLab create?

options.text: 5 jobs — 3 + 2
options.explanation: A matrix is a Cartesian product. Each NODE_VERSION value is combined with each DATABASE value.

options.text: 2 jobs — by the number of variables in the matrix
options.explanation: The number of variables does not define the number of jobs. Jobs equal the number of unique value combinations.

options.text: 1 job with variables — GitLab passes the matrix as an array
options.explanation: No. parallel:matrix creates a separate job for each combination — that is the whole point of matrix execution.

options.text: 6 jobs — 3 x 2 (all combinations)
options.explanation: Correct. parallel:matrix creates all possible combinations. 3 Node versions x 2 databases = 6 jobs: [18,sqlite], [18,postgres], [20,sqlite], [20,postgres], [22,sqlite], [22,postgres].

question: What is the difference between artifacts:reports:junit and artifacts:paths when saving JUnit XML?

options.text: reports:junit signals GitLab to parse XML and show tests in the MR UI; paths simply saves the file for download
options.explanation: Exactly. artifacts:reports is a special type that tells GitLab about the data format. For junit, GitLab shows a Tests tab in the MR with details. paths is just storage without UI integration.

options.text: reports:junit requires a GitLab Premium license, paths is free
options.explanation: Basic JUnit integration is available in the free GitLab plan. Some advanced features (detailed coverage diff) require Premium.

options.text: paths loads faster, reports is slower due to parsing
options.explanation: Load speed is not the key difference. The difference is what GitLab does with the file after saving.

options.text: Both do the same thing, paths is just a more explicit form
options.explanation: These are different mechanisms with different behaviors. reports:junit gives GitLab UI integration. paths is just a file store.

question: You have 4 parallel test shards, each creates junit-1.xml, junit-2.xml, etc. How to correctly collect all reports?

options.text: Add a separate 'merge-reports' job that combines the XML files
options.explanation: GitLab can accept multiple JUnit files directly — no additional merge job is needed.

options.text: GitLab automatically merges all JUnit files without configuration
options.explanation: Not automatically. You must explicitly specify the file list or a glob pattern in artifacts:reports:junit.

options.text: Use a glob pattern: artifacts: reports: junit: 'junit-*.xml'
options.explanation: Correct. GitLab supports glob patterns for reports:junit. All files junit-1.xml, junit-2.xml, etc. will be collected and merged into a single report in the MR UI.

options.text: Save only the last junit file — GitLab reads only one XML
options.explanation: GitLab supports multiple JUnit files (via list or glob). Saving only one loses results from the other shards.

question: E2E tests take 20 minutes and are flaky (sometimes fail for no reason). What is the optimal E2E launch strategy?

options.text: Add allow_failure: true for E2E so flakiness does not block the pipeline
options.explanation: A reasonable temporary approach for flaky tests. allow_failure: true lets the pipeline continue, but GitLab shows a warning. Gives time to fix flakiness without blocking the team.

options.text: Run E2E on a schedule (nightly runs), not on every commit
options.explanation: Good approach for flaky E2E. Nightly runs don't block development, but signal degradation by morning.

options.text: Disable E2E entirely — they are flaky and provide no value
options.explanation: Flakiness is a reason to fix specific tests, not disable E2E. E2E catches integration problems that other test types won't see.

options.text: Run E2E only on commits to main/master and release branches
options.explanation: Correct. E2E on feature branches is usually excessive — unit and integration tests give enough confidence. E2E is needed before production deployment.

options.text: This requires a special license
options.explanation: The listed technologies have open-source versions.

question: You connected the postgres:16 service to a test job. Tests completed successfully, but the database contains data from a previous run. How to fix this?

options.text: GitLab CI service containers are created fresh on each job run — data should not persist
options.explanation: Correct. On each job run, GitLab CI creates a new Docker container for the service. Data is not persistent between runs — if you see 'old data', it is likely created within the same run (test setup/teardown).

options.text: Add cache:key to isolate data between runs
options.explanation: Cache has nothing to do with PostgreSQL data. Cache is used for files on disk (node_modules, etc.).

options.text: Use tmpfs for the database: PGDATA=/tmp/pgdata
options.explanation: This may speed up PostgreSQL, but doesn't solve the nonexistent 'old data' problem — they are deleted along with the container anyway.

options.text: Specify volumes: [] to prohibit data persistence
options.explanation: By default service containers do not mount persistent volumes. Data in PostgreSQL is stored in container memory and deleted with it.

question: What happens if you specify a coverage regex that does not match any line in the test output?

options.text: GitLab will show 0% as the default value
options.explanation: 0% and 'no data' are different states. When the regex doesn't match, data is simply absent, not equal to zero.

options.text: The job fails with error 'coverage pattern not found'
options.explanation: GitLab does not fail a job due to coverage regex mismatch. It simply means no coverage data is available.

options.text: GitLab simply will not show coverage data — no badge, no value in the MR
options.explanation: Correct. If the regex does not match, GitLab ignores coverage — does not show a badge, does not save history. No error, but no data either. This is a common cause of 'missing' coverage in projects.

options.text: GitLab automatically tries another regex from a list of standard ones
options.explanation: GitLab has no list of fallback regexes. Only the regex specified in the config is used.

question: What is the key difference between services in GitLab CI and services in GitHub Actions in terms of network access?

options.text: GitHub Actions does not support services for PostgreSQL — only Redis and MySQL
options.explanation: GitHub Actions supports any Docker images in services, including PostgreSQL. There are no image restrictions.

options.text: In GitLab services are available by image name in an isolated Docker network; in GitHub Actions services forward ports to the runner's localhost
options.explanation: Exactly. GitLab CI: host = image name (postgres, redis), port = standard service port. GitHub Actions: host = localhost or 127.0.0.1, port = as specified in ports. This is important when migrating configs between platforms.

options.text: In both cases services are available as localhost — the platforms are identical
options.explanation: This is wrong. The difference in the network model is one reason why GitLab CI and GitHub Actions configs are not interchangeable.

options.text: GitLab CI does not support services — you need to run dependencies manually via before_script
options.explanation: GitLab CI supports services since version 8.7. This is an official feature, not requiring manual launch.

question: You want to run integration tests only when files in the backend/ directory change. How to set this up in GitLab CI?

options.text: Use only:changes with the pattern 'backend/**/*'
options.explanation: only:changes works, but is deprecated syntax. It is recommended to use rules:changes instead of only/except.

options.text: Use rules:changes to specify paths that should trigger the job
options.explanation: Correct. rules:changes is the modern and flexible approach. When files matching the pattern 'backend/**/*' change, the job runs. It can be combined with other rules conditions for precise control.

options.text: Use the CI_COMMIT_CHANGED_FILES variable in a script condition
options.explanation: This variable does not exist in GitLab CI. For conditional execution based on changed files, use rules:changes.

options.text: Add a script in before_script that checks git diff and exits with 0 if no changes
options.explanation: This is an antipattern. The job will be created and run every time, just exit quickly. The correct approach — don't create the job at all via rules:changes.
